name: Femi Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a large iron ore mine, loading at the shovel and taking rock to the crusher. I've got a vocational certificate and twenty years of reading the road by the tyres and the engine note. My wife Lila works three days a week at a bakery; our two children are still in school, and the mortgage takes most of my mine pay. We have roughly four months of expenses set aside. I don't use AI tools; I keep a small notebook because I trust a mark I made myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift the form is only a form. A computer can tidy a form, but it can't take my truck up a wet ramp. Keep the maintenance checks and the driving as they are, I would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't trust the company to leave a saving alone once it spots one. Even a little automation might mean less overtime, and Lila's bakery hours won't cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on driving and keep my paper fault notes beside the official log. In the first year I'd stop adding optional work to the house and put the spare pay against the mortgage, month by month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not frightened by a quicker form. I'm tired of every small saving becoming another reason to squeeze a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your notebook catch that a routine form misses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The note matters when a warning light comes and goes before a mechanic sees it. I show my foreman the time and the sound I heard, not a guess from software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expense would you pause at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my wife Lila we can wait on repainting the kitchen. I'd rather see the mortgage balance fall than have a new colour on the wall.

say: I'd say **A quicker form** will not drive a loaded truck up a wet ramp.
I would ask the shift to **keep checks** and driving routines that already protect us.
think: I think even a **small saving** may become a reason for management to trim overtime.
I think the mortgage relies on my **mine pay**, since my wife works only three bakery days each week.
do: **Keep driving** and note fleeting truck faults in my paper book alongside the official log.
**Pay down** the mortgage monthly instead of taking on optional house work during the first year.
feel: **Wary** of pressure on hours, even though the picture leaves the driving job largely intact.
S0.quote: A computer can tidy a form, but it can't take my truck up a wet ramp.
fieldNote: His **paper notebook** represents personal responsibility for faults that may vanish before inspection.
Even in a plateau, his **overtime worry** remains because the mortgage depends on mine pay.

steps.text: Keep driving and record truck faults in a paper notebook
Pay extra toward the mortgage instead of repainting the kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can use its new planning software, but someone still has to judge the haul road. I would want the foreman to ask drivers before a route gets changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine may remove dispatch clerks first and then put more loads on each driver. I don't like being measured by a screen that hasn't sat in my cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my notebook to the monthly safety meeting and ask the foreman to check route changes with the drivers. In the first year of new planning software, I'd keep my driving shifts and save the extra pay from busy weeks rather than spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm tense about being pushed harder, though I don't expect a robot in the cab right away. A packed shift is dangerous even without anybody losing a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a route looks unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the software calls the lower ramp open after a downpour, I'd stop and tell dispatch it is unsafe. I won't put a truck on the wet lower ramp to keep a target green.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else could be affected before drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch clerk Mara has a family too, and I would ask whether the mine plans to keep her. Losing a desk job can still make the whole shift work worse.

say: I'd say **Office planning** may change first, but drivers must check routes against the actual haul road.
I would ask the foreman to **consult drivers** before a route change reaches our cabs.
think: I think dispatch jobs may shrink and **load targets** may rise for those still driving.
I think a **screen target** cannot feel how a heavy truck handles after rain.
do: **Bring fault notes** to monthly safety meetings and ask drivers to review route changes.
**Save busy-week pay** in the first year rather than assume the overtime will last.
feel: **Tense** about heavier shifts and safety pressure, even before capable robots reach the cab.
S1.quote: I won't put a truck on the wet lower ramp to keep a target green.
fieldNote: He sees **dispatch clerks** exposed before drivers, but expects drivers to face more loads.
His **response** is through safety meetings and savings, consistent with his reluctance to use AI himself.

steps.text: Bring truck fault notes to monthly driver safety meetings
Save extra pay from busy driving weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 is a threat to dispatch and paperwork first, while the truck robots in this picture come around 2031. I want the mine to say plainly what it plans for drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our overtime could vanish sooner than the driving job, and then the job itself might go when the robots are ready. Four months of savings is not four years of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop the kitchen work and put every second overtime cheque into the savings account. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd ask the foreman and drivers' committee for written numbers on truck plans and possible driver posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lie awake when I picture a silent line of trucks and no roster with my name on it. I can still make a plan, but I need someone to tell the truth about the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which family cost would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first cut would be the kitchen, then our paid weekend trips. I would leave the children's school costs alone as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a different post at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the foreman whether a person will still inspect tyres and brakes before a robot leaves the yard. If those posts are real and keep a decent wage, I'd consider applying.

say: I'd say **Thinking AI** could change dispatch in 2028, with capable truck robots following around 2031.
I would demand **plain truck plans** from the mine before people make decisions about their families.
think: I think **Overtime** could disappear before driving posts do, leaving the mortgage exposed.
I think four months of savings cannot cover **years of payments** if the truck roster goes.
do: **Bank overtime** now and pause kitchen work to build a larger household cushion.
**Request written plans** through the drivers committee in the first year after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible lost hours and eventual job loss, though he can still make a plan.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is not four years of mortgage payments.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 desk changes** from possible hands-on truck replacement around 2031.
The **mortgage** drives both his savings decision and his demand for a real timetable through the drivers committee.

steps.text: Bank every second overtime cheque in the household savings account
Ask the drivers committee for written truck staffing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 gives us five years to make the company put its plans on paper. Robots that can drive like people come around 2034 in this picture, so there should be time for fair notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could imagine checking the trucks before a run, but I won't promise my family a job that has not been offered. I'd rather keep the same mine and the same neighbours than chase a rumour elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the foreman what the inspection posts pay and what certificate they need. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd apply for a truck inspection post if it is staffed by experienced drivers and keeps close to my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried but less cornered than in the fast picture. Five years lets me ask questions while I still have wages coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you taking an inspection post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the inspection wage is much lower, I would stay on the driving roster as long as it exists. We have two children and a mortgage; pride cannot pay either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your wife about that possibility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Lila the inspection idea is only a possibility until we see a wage sheet. She would ask the same question I would: can we keep the house?

say: I'd say **Five years** gives drivers time to demand written staffing plans before truck robots might arrive around 2034.
I would ask for **fair notice** and wages for any inspection posts.
think: I would prefer the **same mine** and community, but an inspection post is only a possibility.
I think a steep **pay cut** would leave the mortgage and two children too exposed.
do: **Ask the foreman** this year about inspection wages and required certificates.
**Apply for** a truck inspection post after thinking AI arrives only if experienced drivers can qualify at close pay.
feel: **Worried**, with more room to ask questions while driving wages continue.
S3.quote: I won't promise my family a job that has not been offered.
fieldNote: His **conditional application** depends on a real inspection vacancy, eligibility and pay near his current wage.
He favours **local continuity** over a speculative move, matching his cautious approach and family commitments.

steps.text: Ask the foreman about inspection post wages and certificates
Apply for an available inspection post if qualified and pay stays close

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2036 is enough warning for the mine to plan honestly with the workforce. The thinking work changes then and the hands-on truck robots follow around 2039, when I'll be in my mid fifties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to finish most of the mortgage before robots arrive. I don't fancy starting another trade in my fifties, and I don't trust a promise that every driver becomes a technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make an extra mortgage payment each quarter from now on, as long as Lila's bakery hours hold. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd ask for a written retirement estimate and compare it with the driving roster before deciding whether to bring retirement forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe with ten years in front of me. I would still grieve the work if the trucks no longer needed drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would extra mortgage payments empty your emergency fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep our four months of emergency savings untouched while paying the mortgage faster. One injury or a short closure could still happen before any of these machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you tell your child about your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son asked whether I would always drive a truck. I told him the truth about work. No one gets an always, but a good working life ought to leave a family with a home.

say: I'd say **Ten years** should be enough for the mine to plan with drivers before capable truck robots might arrive around 2039.
I would ask for **honest plans** rather than promises that every driver can become a technician.
think: I may clear most of the **mortgage** before robots reach the trucks, if household hours hold.
I think starting a **new trade** in my mid fifties does not appeal to me.
do: **Pay extra** on the mortgage each quarter if bakery hours hold, while preserving our emergency savings.
**Compare retirement figures** with the driving roster in the first year after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Calmer** with planning time, and sad at the possible end of a working life in the cab.
S4.quote: No one gets an always, but a good working life ought to leave a family with a home.
fieldNote: He uses the **decade** to reduce mortgage exposure, subject to continued bakery hours.
His **retirement choice** remains conditional on written figures and the roster; he has not committed to retiring early.

steps.text: Pay extra on the mortgage each quarter if bakery hours hold, while keeping emergency savings
Compare written retirement figures with the driving roster after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because overtime could go before the truck does, and then robots might arrive around 2031. Written staffing plans and fair notice would help us choose what to pay down while we still have wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks the truck before it moves without a driver. A quiet truck yard would sound like lost wages to me. I want an actual person named on that check, not a box ticked by a distant screen.

headlineQuote: A quiet truck yard would sound like lost wages to me.
portrait: **Femi Reyes**, 43, drives haul trucks at a large mine and supports two school-age children with his wife.
His **vocational certificate** and long driving experience sit beside a paper notebook; he does not use AI tools.
With a **mortgage** and four months of savings, even lost overtime matters before any robot reaches a truck.
He asks for **written plans**, protects emergency savings and considers inspection work only at a viable wage.
The longer picture gives him time to **reduce debt** and compare retirement figures without assuming a new job exists.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because lost overtime could precede truck robot replacement around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing plans** and fair notice would let his family decide what to pay down while wages continue.
